idiom_name: policy enforcement point (interceptor) in front of the decision point (PDP) backed by a policy store
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: put a single policy enforcement point (PEP) in front of every protected operation - the request filter, middleware, guard, dispatcher or AOP interceptor of the host framework - and have it request one policy decision instead of evaluating rules itself. The policy decision point (PDP) receives the trusted subject, action and resource, consults a policy store or external PDP for RBAC, ABAC or relationship rules, and returns allow or deny; a separate failure handler maps denial to 401/403 and records a privacy-safe audit event. Add an explicit deny-by-default fallback so an unlisted path is closed, keep the pure decision logic free of I/O where possible, and fail closed on policy-store errors. The PAP (Policy Administration Point) is the out-of-band surface where policies are authored, reviewed and published; separating PAP from runtime PDP enables policy updates without redeploying handlers.
code_sketch:
request -> [PEP] --(trusted subject, action, resource)--> [PDP]
                         |                                      |
                         |                                [policy store]
                         v
                  allow -> handler
                  deny/error -> 401/403 + audit (stop)
# fallback: deny when no rule matches
pitfalls: Putting role checks in each handler -> callers drift and an overlooked path stays open -> keep the rule in the PDP and let the PEP enforce its result.
Leaving unmatched requests at default allow -> every new endpoint starts public -> configure an explicit denyAll/fallback rule and test it.

Trusting roles, tenant IDs or resource IDs supplied by the client -> the caller can widen its own permissions or read another object -> derive subject and policy attributes from validated server-side context.
Failing open when the PDP times out or returns an error -> a policy outage becomes an authorization outage in the attacker's favour -> deny and emit an operational signal.
Caching allow decisions without bounded TTL or revocation invalidation -> a removed permission remains usable -> cache only with an explicit freshness and invalidation contract.
Putting the only PEP at an API gateway -> internal service calls or worker paths bypass it -> enforce again at each service boundary that owns protected data.

Checking only a URL or role before loading an object -> BOLA/IDOR and tenant-crossing reads remain possible -> include the resource and tenant in the decision or enforce ownership in the domain layer.
Logging a denial and then continuing, or deciding after a write -> the forbidden side effect still happens -> return 401/403 before mutation and stop the pipeline.
Treating a coarse boundary check as complete mediation -> fine-grained object or field access is left unchecked -> add resource-level enforcement for operations whose policy needs loaded state.
